title: "When you should not scale time series for nonlinear analysis"
description: "Population and community time series are often scaled (mean-centered and scaled by standard deviation) before analysis. While this works with linear models, it does not with nonlinear analysis. This also depends on whether you analyze on linear or on log-scale."

```{r}
#| echo: false
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")
# theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))
```




## Linear and nonlinear analysis

Linear time series analysis is popular with observed time series of community abundances from the field. Classically, a multivariate time series of $n$ species $X_t=(x_{1,t},\dots,x_{n,t})$ is log-transformed $Y_t=\log(X_t)$, before a multivariate autoregressive model **MAR(1)** is fitted
$$
y_{i,t+1}=y_{i,t} + a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}y_{j,t}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t}
$$
With matrix algebra, this can be written as
$$
Y_{t+1}=Y_{t} + A+BY_{t}+CU_{t} + \varepsilon_{t}
$$
where $B$ is an interaction matrix, and $C$ contains the effects of environmental variables $U_t$. This model is purely linear. [Something about SSM, MARSS package, etc]
```{r}

```


This MAR(1) model actually corresponds to an ecological community model. If we transform densities back to the original scale, we get the discrete-time, multi-species **Gompertz** model.  
$$
\begin{align}
x_{i,t+1} &=x_{i,t} \cdot \exp\left( a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\textcolor{red}{y_{j,t}}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \right) \\
&=x_{i,t} \cdot \exp\left( a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\textcolor{red}{\log(x_{j,t})}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 100%

n = 1000
x = seq(.01, 2, length.out=n)
y = log(x)

# Gompertz model

a =  0.04
b = -0.1

df = data.frame(x = x, 
                y = a+b*y)
p1 = ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, lty=3) +
  xlab("Density x") +
  ylab("Growth rate") +
  ggtitle("Gompertz")

df = data.frame(x = y, 
                y = a+b*y)
p2 = ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, lty=3) +
  xlab("log(Density) y") +
  ylab("Growth rate") +
  ggtitle("Gompertz on logscale")

p1 + p2
```



More common in modeling, however, is the generalized Lotka-Volterra model. In its discrete-time version, the **Ricker** model, it reads
$$
x_{i,t+1} =x_{i,t} \cdot \exp\left( a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\textcolor{red}{x_{j,t}}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \right) 
$$
On logscale, it becomes an additive model just as the Gompertz, although it is not linear in $y$ anymore. However, it is still linear in its parameters, and by defining new predictors $\exp(y_i)$, we could still push it through `lm(...)` to estimate all parameters [link to blog post]. 
$$
\begin{align}
y_{i,t+1} &=y_{i,t} +  a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\textcolor{red}{x_{j,t}}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \\
&=y_{i,t} +  a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\textcolor{red}{\exp(y_{j,t})}+\sum_{j=1}^m c_{ij}u_{j,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \\
\end{align}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 100%

n = 1000
x = seq(.01, 2, length.out=n)
y = log(x)

# Ricker model

a = 0.5   
b = -0.3333

df = data.frame(x = x, 
                y = a+b*x)
p1 = ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, lty=3) +
  xlab("Density x") +
  ylab("Growth rate") +
  ggtitle("Ricker")

df = data.frame(x = y, 
                y = a+b*x)
p2 = ggplot(df, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, lty=3) +
  xlab("log(Density) y") +
  ylab("Growth rate") +
  ggtitle("Ricker on logscale")

p1 + p2
```


## Scaling and reparametrization

For the linear MAR(1) / **Gompertz** model, it makes sense to scale log-transformed observations $y_{i,t}$ species-wise, i.e., $\tilde y_{i,t}=\frac{y_{i,t}-\text{mean}(y_i)}{\text{sd}(y_i)}$. This effectively is a reparametrization of the model, with parameter estimates describing relative interaction strength. Setting up the MAR(1) equations for the scaled variables, we get
$$
\begin{align}
\tilde y_{i,t+1} &= \tilde y_{i,t} + \tilde a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij} \tilde y_{j,t}+\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
\frac{y_{i,t+1}-\mu_i}{\sigma_i} &= \frac{y_{i,t}-\mu_i}{\sigma_i} + \tilde a_i +\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij}  \frac{y_{j,t}-\mu_j}{\sigma_j} +\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t}
\end{align}
$$
Now multiplying both sides by $\sigma_i$ and rearranging coefficients, we get the MAR(1) equations for the original log-abundances $y_{i,t}$.
$$
\begin{align}
y_{i,t+1} &= y_{i,t+1} + \sigma_i\tilde a_i +\sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_i\tilde b_{ij}  \frac{y_{j,t}-\mu_j}{\sigma_j} +\sum_{j=1}^m \sigma_i\tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
&= y_{i,t+1} + \underbrace{\sigma_i\tilde a_i - \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_j}\tilde b_{ij} \mu_j }_{:= a_i}  + \sum_{j=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_j}\tilde b_{ij}}_{:=b_{ij}}  y_{j,t}  +\sum_{j=1}^m \underbrace{\sigma_i\tilde c_{ij}}_{:=c_{ij}}u_{j,t} \\
&=  y_{i,t} +  a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n  b_{ij}  y_{j,t}+\sum_{j=1}^m  c_{ij}u_{j,t}
\end{align}
$$

This only worked because the Gompertz model is, on logscale, linear both in the parameters as well as the state variables.

It does not work the same way for the **Ricker** model. Here, reparameterization is only feasible for mean-centering $\tilde y_{i,t}=y_{i,t}-\text{mean}(y_i)$.

$$
\begin{align}
\tilde y_{i,t+1} &= \tilde y_{i,t} + \tilde a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij} \exp(\tilde y_{j,t})+\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
{y_{i,t+1}-\mu_i} &= {y_{i,t}-\mu_i} + \tilde a_i +\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij}  \exp({y_{j,t}-\mu_j}) +\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
{y_{i,t+1}} &= {y_{i,t}} + \underbrace{\tilde a_i}_{:= a_i} +\sum_{j=1}^n  \underbrace{\frac{\tilde b_{ij}}{\exp(\mu_j)}}_{:=b_{ij}}   \exp({y_{j,t}}) +\sum_{j=1}^m \underbrace{\tilde c_{ij}}_{:=c_{ij}}u_{j,t} \\
&=  y_{i,t} +  a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n  b_{ij}  \exp(y_{j,t})+\sum_{j=1}^m  c_{ij}u_{j,t}
\end{align}
$$

However, scaling $\tilde y_{i,t}=\frac{y_{i,t}}{\text{sd}(y_i)}$ we get stuck.

$$
\begin{align}
\tilde y_{i,t+1} &= \tilde y_{i,t} + \tilde a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij} \exp(\tilde y_{j,t})+\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
\frac{y_{i,t+1}}{\sigma_i} &= \frac{y_{i,t+1}}{\sigma_i} + \tilde a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n \tilde b_{ij} \exp\left(\frac{y_{j,t}}{\sigma_i}\right)+\sum_{j=1}^m \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} \\
y_{i,t+1} &= y_{i,t+1} + \sigma_i\tilde a_i+\sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_i \tilde b_{ij} \exp(y_{j,t})^{1/ \sigma_i}+\sum_{j=1}^m \sigma_i \tilde c_{ij}u_{j,t} 
\end{align}
$$
The nonlinear transformation of the Ricker-predictors $\exp(y_{j,t})$ (raised to the power $1/\sigma_i$), does not allow us to transform these equations back to the original Ricker model by reparameterization of the model coefficients.

## Conclusions

When fitting an linear MAR(1) on log-scaled population abundances $y_{i,t}$ we can indeed mean-center and sd-scale the data. The result is still a Gompertz community model, and parameters for the non-scaled abundances can be obtained by simple transformations.

The same holds for mean-centered data in the Ricker model. However, when also sd-scaling the data, we are not fitting a Ricker model anymore. Estimated parameters cannot be transformed back to the coefficients of generalized Lotka-Volterra model.
